stories.title: Tarps in Technicolor: Meet Artist Sasi Chambers before the MKE Studio Tour
stories.summary: Sasi Chambers invented her own art form: 'tarpage' — collage on discarded tarps, layered with duct tape, marker, beads, and sequins. This weekend, the MKE Studio Tour opens her Milwaukee makerspace to the public for the first time.
stories.extended_summary: Sasi Chambers makes art out of what everyone else throws away. Her medium is 'tarpage' — a word she coined, blending 'tarp' and 'collage' — built on polyvinyl tarps found discarded outdoors, then layered with duct tape, permanent marker, hand-sewn beads, and sequins. The result is technicolor and unorthodox: raindrops, 'flame drops,' soulful eyes, lightning, snakes, weird clouds. 'I've always been drawn to the less functional, more interesting things; to colors and patterns,' she says. After a career as a public art installationist in Boise, Chambers moved to Milwaukee in 2023. On Oct. 3–4, she opens her makerspace as part of the MKE Studio Tour — her first public showing since the move, and a decade's worth of tarpages on display.

stories.title: There and Back Again
stories.summary: At 12:56 a.m., 21-year-old Oliver Levine pushed off into pitch darkness on a 12-foot paddleboard — and didn't stop for 48 miles. He became only the second person ever to paddle across Monterey Bay and back, on a board far smaller than the first.
stories.extended_summary: At 12:56 a.m. on September 9, 21-year-old UC Santa Cruz student Oliver Levine pushed off from Cowells Beach into total darkness — alone, on a 12-foot board, with no support boat and only a barely-working VHF radio. About a mile offshore, bioluminescent plankton lit up the water around him. 'Your mind processes every little thing as a threat,' he says. 'Paddling alone at night out there… it's not fun.' Twelve hours and 48 miles later, he landed back home, becoming only the second person ever to complete a full lap of Monterey Bay — over a trench deeper than the Grand Canyon. The first did it on an 18-foot board. Levine chose a stock 12-footer, because it takes far more energy. 'Part of me wanted to take the challenge a step further.'
